text.en: A farmer has an ox but needs shoes, a sweater and medicines. One person offers shoes, another a sweater, a third medicines, and none of them wants an ox. Meanwhile, in your class, your classmate has forgotten an eraser but has an extra pencil, and you have the eraser. You swap, and you both are happy. This is barter. How did people move from swapping things to using money? Let us find out.

Barter means exchanging goods and services directly for other goods and services without using money. A transaction is a piece of business done between people to buy and sell. Barter works only when each person wants what the other has, a problem called the double coincidence of wants. If one person feels the exchange is disadvantageous, he will not agree. Other problems arise: in what proportion should two goods be exchanged? How do you split an ox into small parts without destroying it? How do you store what you receive? Bags of wheat rot or get eaten by rats, so the capacity to be stored for a long time, called durability, matters. Barter has not completely disappeared. People of the hills exchange produce for rice cakes with people from the plains at the Junbeel Mela in Morigaon, Assam, held every year. Old clothes are exchanged for new utensils, and children may barter books in a book exchange.
People looked for a common medium of exchange that everybody accepted. For a long time they used commodities such as cowrie shells, salt, tea, tobacco, cloth, cattle, seeds and even feather coils. The Aztec copper Tajadero, a chopping knife, was used as money in central Mexico, and in the Solomon Islands people used Tevau, red feather coils made from birds' feathers. Money is anything accepted by everyone as payment. It must be accepted widely, divisible, durable and easy to carry and store.
Metal coins came next. Because metals last and can be divided and carried, they were ideal. Coins were made of precious metals such as gold, silver and copper or their alloys. An alloy is a mixture of metals. Coins today are alloys consisting largely of iron. Ancient Indian rulers issued coins, and different kingdoms had their own coinage, carrying symbols on the obverse (head) and reverse (tail). Roman gold coins found in Pudukottai in Tamil Nadu show that Indian merchants traded with Rome. Scholars conclude that trade was in India's favour because many Roman coins were found here. Coinage helped to boost India's maritime trade with the world. Ancient laws also fixed penalties in coins, for example the fine for failing to help a neighbour was 100 panas.
Metal coins are heavy to carry in large amounts. The search for a more convenient form ended with paper money, first issued in India by banks such as the Bank of Bengal and the Bank of Bombay. Today the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the only legal source that prints and distributes paper notes. Coins are used for smaller denominations, and notes for larger ones. Denominations are the units in which coins and notes are classified. Currency is the form of money that a country issues. The rupee sign was adopted by the Government of India in 2010.
With new technology people use debit cards, credit cards, net banking and UPI, the Unified Payments Interface, to pay without carrying cash. The limits of barter led to money as a medium of exchange, and forms of money have changed with time: shells, coins, paper notes, and digital payments.

problem.en: A farmer wants to swap wheat for shoes, but the shoemaker wants a sweater, not wheat. Which problem is this and how does money solve it?

text.en: Each side must want what the other has: this is the double coincidence of wants.
With money the farmer sells wheat to anyone and buys shoes from the shoemaker.
So both transactions can happen separately.

why.en: Money splits one exchange into two.

prompt.en: Why did people move from barter to coins and then to paper money?

requiredIdeas.en: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants.
Goods are hard to divide or store.
Coins and notes are durable, divisible and widely accepted.

points.en: Barter has limits: double coincidence of wants, divisibility, storage.
Money is a common medium of exchange.
Money evolved from commodities to coins to paper notes to digital payments.
The RBI issues notes in India.
